title: Time and Money
bigQuestion: How do clocks and coins help us know what time it is and how much we have?

story.title: The Clock and the Cash Box
story.kicker: One clock on the wall and one box of coins run the whole day in Room 12.
paragraphs: Every morning in Room 12, Dev looks at the clock over the door. The short hand points at the 9. The long hand points at the 12. It is 9:00. That means lunch count time. Dev counts hands. Twelve kids want hot lunch. He writes 12 on the slip.

The clock keeps going. At 9:30 the long hand points down at the 6. Reading time. At 10:15 the long hand is on the 3. Math time. Dev likes to say the times out loud. His teacher says the clock is a map of the day.

On Friday the class holds a bake sale. Cookies cost 25 cents. Juice costs 50 cents. Dev sits by the cash box. A girl hands him three dimes for a cookie. He counts: 10, 20, 30. That is more than 25. He counts up from 25 to 30. He gives her back a nickel.

At 3:00 p.m. the bell rings. Dev counts the cash box. Quarters first, then dimes, then nickels, then pennies. The class made $6.75. The clock said the day was over. The coins said the sale was a success.
story.think: Why did Dev count the quarters before the pennies?

lessons.title: Hour and Half Hour
lessons.mainIdea: The short hand tells the hour. Long hand on 12 means o'clock; long hand on 6 means half past.
reading: A clock has two hands. The short hand is the *hour hand*. The long hand is the *minute hand*. When the long hand points to 12, it is o'clock. Short hand on 3, long hand on 12: 3 o'clock. We write 3:00.
When the long hand points to 6, it is *half past*. The short hand sits between two numbers. It is between 3 and 4, so it is half past 3. We write 3:30. Thirty minutes is half an hour.
A digital clock shows only numbers. 3:00 means 3 o'clock. 3:30 means half past 3. Watch out: at 3:30 the short hand is past the 3, not on it. Use the number it just passed.

words.d: the short hand on a clock; it points to the hour
the long hand on a clock; it shows the minutes
30 minutes after the hour; the long hand points to the 6

look.title: The Clock on the Wall
look.text: Look at the clock on the wall. The short hand is between the 7 and the 8. The long hand points straight down at the 6. The class is just finishing breakfast.
look.prompt: What time is it? How do you write it with numbers?

check.q: The short hand is on 5. The long hand is on 12. What time is it?
check.why: Long hand on 12 means o'clock. Short hand on 5 means 5. So it is 5:00.

check.q: The short hand is between 8 and 9. The long hand is on 6. What time is it?
check.why: Long hand on 6 means half past. The short hand passed the 8, so it is 8:30.

check.q: How many minutes are in half an hour?
check.why: An hour is 60 minutes. Half of 60 is 30.

lessons.title: Five Minutes at a Time
lessons.mainIdea: Each number on the clock is 5 minutes. Count by fives from the 12.
reading: The long hand moves around the clock. Each number it passes is 5 *minutes*. Count by fives from the 12. At the 1 it is 5 minutes. At the 2 it is 10. At the 3 it is 15. At the 6 it is 30.
Short hand just past 2, long hand on the 4. Count: 5, 10, 15, 20. It is 2:20. Short hand near 10, long hand on the 9. Count: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45. It is 9:45.
Read the short hand first. Use the number it passed. Then count the long hand by fives. A common mistake is reading the long hand as 4 instead of 20. The number is a helper, not the minutes.

words.d: a short bit of time; 60 minutes make one hour

look.title: Where the Long Hand Points
look.cite: Counting by fives around a clock face
look.prompt: The long hand is on the 7. How many minutes is that?

check.q: The long hand points to the 8. How many minutes past the hour is it?
check.why: Count by fives to the 8: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40. It is 40 minutes.

check.q: The short hand is just past 4. The long hand is on the 2. What time is it?
check.why: The hour is 4. Long hand on the 2 is 5, 10. So it is 4:10.

check.q: The short hand is near 6. The long hand is on the 11. What time is it?
check.why: The hour is 6. Count by fives to the 11: 11 fives is 55. So it is 6:55.

lessons.title: Morning, Noon and Night
lessons.mainIdea: A.M. is morning, before noon. P.M. is afternoon and evening, after noon.
reading: A day has 24 hours. The clock goes around twice. *A.M.* means the hours from midnight to noon. *P.M.* means the hours from noon to midnight. 7:00 a.m. is breakfast time. 7:00 p.m. is close to bedtime.
Look at a school day. School starts at 8:30 a.m. Lunch is at 12:00. That is *noon*. Recess is at 1:15 p.m. School ends at 3:00 p.m. Dinner is at 6:00 p.m.
A schedule is a list of times. It tells what comes next. Reading is at 9:00 a.m. Math is at 10:00 a.m. Math comes after reading. The earlier time always comes first.

words.d: the hours from midnight to noon; the morning
the hours from noon to midnight; afternoon, evening and night
12:00 in the middle of the day, when a.m. changes to p.m.

look.title: One School Day
look.cite: Example schedule for one school day

check.q: You eat breakfast at 7:00. Is it a.m. or p.m.?
check.why: Breakfast is in the morning, before noon. Morning hours are a.m.

check.q: What do we call 12:00 in the middle of the day?
check.why: Noon is 12:00 in the daytime. Midnight is 12:00 at night.

check.q: Music is at 1:00 p.m. Art is at 10:00 a.m. Which comes first?
choices: they are at the same time
check.why: 10:00 a.m. is in the morning. 1:00 p.m. is after noon. Art comes first.

lessons.title: What Each Coin Is Worth
lessons.mainIdea: A penny is 1 cent, a nickel 5 cents, a dime 10 cents, a quarter 25 cents.
reading: A penny is worth 1 *cent*. A nickel is worth 5 cents. A dime is worth 10 cents. A quarter is worth 25 cents. We write cents with a ¢ sign. 5¢ means 5 cents.
Size can fool you. A dime is the smallest *coin*. But it is worth more than a penny or a nickel. A nickel is bigger than a dime but worth less. Look at the coin, not its size.
Two nickels make 10 cents, the same as one dime. 5 + 5 = 10. Five pennies make one nickel. Two dimes and a nickel make 25 cents. 10 + 10 + 5 = 25. That is the same as one quarter.

words.d: the smallest amount of U.S. money; a penny is one cent
a small round piece of metal money, like a penny or a dime

look.title: U.S. Coins
look.prompt: How many nickels make one quarter?

check.q: Which coin is worth 10 cents?
check.why: A dime is 10 cents. A nickel is 5 and a quarter is 25.

check.q: How many pennies equal one nickel?
check.why: A nickel is 5 cents. Five pennies at 1 cent each make 5 cents.

check.q: Which is worth more, a dime or a nickel?
choices: the nickel, because it is bigger
the dime, because it is 10 cents
check.why: A dime is 10 cents and a nickel is 5 cents. The dime is small but worth more.

lessons.title: Counting Mixed Coins
lessons.mainIdea: Start with the biggest coins. Count on by 25, 10, 5, then 1.
reading: Jamal has a quarter, a dime and two pennies. Start with the biggest coin. Quarter: 25. *Count on* with the dime: 35. Add a penny: 36. Add a penny: 37. He has 37 cents.
Sort first. Put quarters, then dimes, then nickels, then pennies. Two dimes and three nickels: 10, 20, then 25, 30, 35. That is 35 cents. Big coins first keeps the numbers easy.
Check by counting a different way. Three nickels are 15. Two dimes are 20. 15 + 20 = 35. Same answer. If your two counts do not match, count again.

words.d: start at one number and keep counting up from there

look.title: Coins in a Hand
look.text: Picture a hand holding coins: one quarter, two dimes, one nickel and one penny. Say the count out loud, big coins first: 25, 35, 45, 50, 51.
look.prompt: How much money is in the hand? Now count it a second way to check.

check.q: One quarter and one dime. How many cents?
Two dimes and one nickel. How many cents?
One quarter, one nickel and two pennies. How many cents?

lessons.title: Money Word Problems
lessons.mainIdea: 100 cents make 1 dollar. Add or subtract cents to solve money problems.
reading: A *dollar* is 100 cents. Four quarters make a dollar: 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 100. We write one dollar as $1.00. We write 45 cents as 45¢ or as $0.45.
Mia buys a pencil for 30¢ and an eraser for 15¢. How much in all? 30 + 15 = 45. She pays 45¢. Kai has 50¢ and spends 20¢. How much is left? 50 − 20 = 30. He has 30¢ left.
Read the question twice. In all means add. Left means subtract. Draw the coins if it helps. Then check your work: 30 + 15 = 45, and 45 − 15 = 30. It matches.

words.d: 100 cents; four quarters or ten dimes make one dollar

look.title: At the Bake Sale Table
look.text: The bake sale sells cookies for 25¢ and juice for 50¢. Priya buys one cookie and one juice. She hands over three quarters and waits.
look.prompt: How much does Priya spend? Did she pay the right amount?

check.q: A sticker costs 40¢. A pencil costs 35¢. How much for both?
check.why: 40 + 35 = 75. Both together cost 75¢.

check.q: Lily has 80¢. She spends 30¢. How much is left?
check.why: 80 − 30 = 50. She has 50¢ left.

check.q: How many quarters make one dollar?
check.why: 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 100 cents, which is one dollar. That is 4 quarters.

lessons.title: Making Change by Counting Up
lessons.mainIdea: To make change, count up from the price to the money paid.
reading: A cookie costs 35¢. Tom pays with two quarters, 50¢. How much *change* does he get? Count up from 35. From 35 to 40 is a nickel. From 40 to 50 is a dime. 5 + 10 = 15. Tom gets 15¢ back.
Check with subtraction. 50 − 35 = 15. Same answer. Counting up is like climbing stairs. Start at the price. Stop at the money paid. The steps you took are the change.
Try another one. Juice is 60¢. Ana pays $1.00. Count up: 60 to 70 is 10. 70 to 100 is 30. 10 + 30 = 40. The change is 40¢. Check: 100 − 60 = 40. Yes.

words.d: the money you get back when you pay more than the price

look.title: A Muffin and Two Quarters
look.text: A muffin costs 45¢. Sam pays with two quarters, which is 50¢. The seller counts up out loud: 45, and one nickel makes 50.
look.prompt: How much change does Sam get? Check it with subtraction.

check.q: A pencil costs 20¢. You pay with a quarter. How much change do you get?
check.why: Count up from 20 to 25. That is 5. Check: 25 − 20 = 5.

check.q: Gum costs 70¢. You pay with $1.00. How much change do you get?
check.why: Count up from 70 to 100. That is 30. Check: 100 − 70 = 30.

check.q: Why do we count up from the price?
choices: to find how many coins we have
check.why: Counting up from the price to the money paid shows how much comes back. That is the change.

review.q: The short hand is on 9. The long hand is on 12. What time is it?
review.why: Long hand on 12 means o'clock. Short hand on 9 means 9:00.

review.q: The long hand points to the 3. How many minutes past the hour is it?
review.why: Count by fives: 5, 10, 15. The 3 means 15 minutes.

review.q: Bedtime is 8:00 at night. Is that a.m. or p.m.?
review.why: Night hours come after noon, so 8:00 at night is p.m.

review.q: One dime and three pennies. How many cents?
A toy costs 60¢. A ball costs 25¢. How much for both?
Bread costs 40¢. You pay 50¢. What is your change?
review.why: Count up from 40 to 50. That is 10. Check: 50 − 40 = 10.
